articles.text: Now that many intelligent observers have gone over our freight route, it is being made known that a very valuable country will be developed by it. The riches of the Bad Lands are spoken of in another article. When the road strikes the ridge, some of the best agricultural land in the territory is found and with few exceptions extends clear to the Hills. Besides the precious metals found here, there is at least one vein of pure hard coal which is now mined extensively and found to equal Pennsylvania coal in every respect. A vein of the purest mica has been found and is now being sold at the mine for $90 a cubic foot. The supply seems inexhaustible. These reasons, besides many others, make it almost certain that a railroad will soon be built. It has been under consideration for some time and as for almost half the distance the road will require no grading whatever and will be immensely remunerative we feel safe in predicting that the road will at least be commenced before six months are passed.
articles.summary: Editorial predicting that a railroad will follow the Medora–Black Hills freight route within six months, citing coal, mica and farmland along the way.

articles.text: A person scarcely thinks he is becoming acquainted with the resources of the Bad Lands when something new is discovered of which he had no previous conception. We have yet to hear of a man who was posted, who did not place the Bad Lands at or near the top of all the cattle countries in the United States. Here the productiveness of the Bad Lands was and still is supposed to stop. On the contrary, it scarcely begins here. By repeated experiments the soil has been found extremely productive and it will raise vegetables in profusion. The strangest thing about the soil is that the tops of the buttes, from two to four hundred feet high, have been found far more productive than the bottom lands. Beyond gardening, however, agriculture will never be a success here on account of the broken nature of the country. To the east and southeast, however, no better land can be found anywhere. The buttes which have hitherto been considered worthless, except for their wealth of coal and the shelter they furnished stock, are now found to be regular gold mines. Red and white brick and potter's clay abound and of a quality unsurpassed in the world. Fire clay, cement, molder's sand and sandstone, all of the very best quality, are in almost every butte. The coal, one to five veins of which can be seen in every [raw?] butte, is the best quality of lignite to be found in Dakota. Beyond all this it is certain that there is a large amount of petroleum in the Bad Lands, as many streams are so thickly covered as to be unfit for drinking. Whether it will pay to sink wells for it is a question which will soon be decided. A great future is certainly in store for the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Editorial on the mineral and agricultural resources of the Bad Lands: productive butte-top soil, clays, cement, lignite and possible petroleum.

articles.headline: Communication.
articles.text:
The following memoranda were handed us by Dr. J. M. Louthan. As our readers will notice it is a very interesting account of a trip made from Deadwood and Spearfish over the now completed Medora freight route to Medora by a party composed of Thos. G. Jones, H. M. Jorgens, E. Deffebach, Dr. J. M. Louthan and Doc. Pennell:

"We started April 1 from Spearfish at 3 P. M. Traveling over the new road to Red Water we found an outfit busily at work on the bridge. The stream was down and we forded it easily. B. Deffebach and myself went over the grade with saddle horses and found the work almost complete on the Red Water hill. The road was dry and dusty from that point to Belle Fourche, where we arrived at 5 P. M. Here we found A. Burnham with a force of ten men and five of Mr. T. G. Jones' teams, constructing a bridge across the Belle Fourche river. The bridge will be finished by April 10 at a cost of $1,500. Fording the Belle Fourche on a good rock bottom, we pulled for Crow creek, where we arrived at 5:30. Here we made an early camp for the night, having plenty of wood and water. After supper, beds were quickly made and we were soundly asleep in the open air.

Daylight of April 2 broke without a cloud. At 6:30 we were on the move. Before reaching the divide between Crow creek and Owl creek a beautiful phenomenon was seen. Looking toward the east we could see a perfect rainbow on the blades of grass, caused by the frost crystals resolving themselves into dew drops. The road was good and perfectly dry between Crow creek and Owl creek where we arrived at 8:30. This will be bridged in a few days, as there is an abundance of wood immediately alongside the trail. At 10 o'clock we headed for Indian creek, arriving there at 12:20 and encamped for dinner. Continuing our course directly north we went into camp for the night on the south fork of the Moreau.

At 8 o'clock of April 3, we crossed the Moreau and found the freight road to Medora. Stopping for dinner near Nash's ranch in the Short Pine hills. One great beauty of the whole road we found was that everywhere there was an abundance of wood and water. At 5:30, we arrived at John Gallop's, where we were hospitably entertained for the night.

At 6 o'clock of April 4 we started on, but Deffebach's Arabian steed, better known as a broncho, concluded to roll. In so doing he turned the saddle, became scared and started for the Cœur D'Alene mines. Rassie, having no faith in that section of the country, concluded he would round the brute up and strike for the Bohemian settlement on the Northern Pacific R. R. All this took up much valuable time of those who were anxious to locate the road from Spearfish to Medora. At 5:30 we arrived at Eagle springs, better known as Foot & Beckett's ranch. This place was located upward of two years ago, and the firm have since kept a hunter's supply store. Buffalo used to be here by the thousands, but now they are all gone. We saw the carcasses of hundreds strewn over the prairies, in some instances neither hide nor meat being taken. Being a sportsman myself, I keenly felt the inevitable fact, as I looked into the dim future, that the time was fast coming when the buffalo, antelope, deer and beaver would pass into the long catalogue of animals that had become extinct. Yet while taking a philosophical view of this seemingly wanton destruction, we could still see before the sunset of our lives great herds of cattle roaming over this vast domain, more profitable to the white man than game of any kind. Taking into consideration that this country, wonderful for its agricultural and grazing resources, is in close proximity to the Sioux reservation, the sooner game is destroyed the less danger there is to the pioneer, who will soon find for his wife and little ones a good home and open up a new country, which will earn himself an independency and lay the foundations for railroads, towns, schools, churches and colleges.

At Eagle springs we found Mr. Palmer and wife in charge of Foot & Beckett's store and eating house. The first person we met being Mr. Jas. Elliott, bookkeeper of the VVV outfit. Mr. Palmer and wife soon had a good supper for us which was heartily enjoyed by the entire party. Mr. Elliott accompanied us for a distance on our way to the railroad.

At 6 o'clock of April 5 we started over a beautiful rolling prairie, and after ten miles pulled up at Mr. Maddox' ranch, located on one of the head streams of the Cannonball river. Here we saw a vein of coal forty feet thick, exposed to view. After making some investigations we found that the whole country was underlaid with coal. After spending some time here, Doc, the scout, misled us to the extent of about eight miles, owing to the fact that the road had been shortened by the locators from Medora some ten or twelve miles.

In the afternoon, when within eight miles of Medora, rain and snow began falling. We soon arrived at Eaton's ranch, however, and were cordially entertained by Mr. Eaton, who told us that his sons were at Little Missouri, attending the stock meeting. In the morning, bidding good-by to Mr. Eaton, who is one of God's noblemen, we soon arrived at our destination—Medora, the future great.

During our whole journey we did not change horses and the time actually consumed in travelling was a little less than three days and a half. Nearly the whole way the road was dry and dusty, and the distance from Medora to Spearfish is not an inch over 160 miles."
articles.summary: Dr. J. M. Louthan's account of a party's trip from Spearfish over the new Medora freight route, April 1–6, 1884.

articles.headline: Round-Up Meeting.
articles.text:
The meeting to arrange for the round-up of the Little Missouri river and tributaries was held, in accordance with the call, last Saturday, April 5, in Pennell & Roberts' hall, at Little Missouri, Dak.

The meeting was called to order at 2:30 by H. S. Boice, who nominated B. Barr for chairman. No other nominations being made, Mr. Barr was declared unanimously elected. Howard Eaton nominated A. T. Packard for secretary, who was also unanimously elected.

C. W. Sleeper moved that the chair appoint a delegate from each range to arrange for a round-up, seconded by G. Grisy. Mr. Boice moved to amend by having the chair appoint a committee of seven; J. L. Truscott seconded. Carried. The committee as appointed was: G. W. Towers, C. W. Sleeper, H. S. Boice, M. Wadsworth, Howard Eaton, Wm. Merrifield and G. Grisy. Howard Eaton resigning, W. L. Eaton was appointed in his stead.

Howard Eaton moved for a recess until the committee made their report. Carried.

After an adjournment of half an hour the meeting was called to order and listened to the following report:

"Your committee would recommend that the round-up for this district commence on May 25, at the crossing of the Northern Pacific R. R. of the Big Beaver at Keith, and hunt down to the mouth of the Big Beaver. Thence move up the Little Missouri, working tributaries to the mouth of the Little Beaver, sending a small party over to the headwaters of the Knife and Green rivers. Thence up the Little Beaver and cross over to the head of the Big Beaver, working tributaries, and thence down to the point of starting at the railroad crossing of the Big Beaver. We would also recommend that John Goodall be appointed captain or foreman of this round-up and that Wm. Jones be appointed assistant, and that the foreman have full control of this round-up with authority to discharge any men who refuse to obey orders.

(Signed) G. W. TOWERS,
C. W. SLEEPER,
H. S. BOICE,
M. WADSWORTH,
W. L. EATON,
WM. MERRIFIELD,
G. GRISY."

Howard Eaton moved that the report be adopted. Carried.

G. Grisy moved that copies of THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, containing a report of this meeting, be sent to the Miles City Association. Carried.

Adjourned.

B. BARR, Chairman.
A. T. PACKARD, Secretary.
articles.summary: Minutes of the April 5 meeting at Little Missouri that set the Little Missouri round-up to start May 25 at Keith, with John Goodall as foreman.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. Call for Bad Lands Association.

CALL FOR BAD LANDS ASSOCIATION.

There will be a meeting held at Little Missouri crossing, the third Monday in April (the 21st) for the purpose of forming a Bad Lands Association. All raisers of live stock are requested to attend. Upon its organization, business of much importance will come before the association and it is to the interest of every man interested in live stock to attend.

THE COMMITTEE.

articles.text:
It is a significant fact that meetings are being held in various parts of England to protest against the severity of the restrictions relative to the importation of foreign cattle contemplated in the contagious disease act, now before parliament.—[Western Rural.

R. M. Sparks, Lexington, Mo., a prominent breeder and owner of a cattle ranch at Medicine Lodge, Kan., who has considerable practical experience with diseased cattle, informs The Kansas Farmer that he has read everything published concerning the new cattle disease in that state and is confident that it was nothing more than grease heel.

Great mortality prevails among the horses in different sections of Oregon. The disease prevalent seems to be blind staggers. A large percentage of cases result fatally, and the disease baffles the skill of the most experienced veterinary surgeons. Soon after contracting the disease the animal becomes partially or totally blind, is unable to walk, swells up and dies. The greatest mortality prevails in Chicamas and Yam Hill counties. Over 500 valuable horses have died recently in these counties. The disease is seriously interfering with farmers' seeding. It is contagious and at our latest accounts it was spreading.—[Western Farmer.

This time last year a Barber county cattleman was a most abject and miserable appearing being; his face was long and sour; his words were few and doleful, and he appeared to have lost his last friend. How different now! He capers nimbly on sleek fat horses; his face is wreathed in smiles; he luxuriates in ten-cent cigars and fine-cut tobacco; takes hot hotel dinners when he comes to town and would as soon talk of selling his family as his cows. Last year he was wondering if he would have cattle enough to pay the round-up expenses, and this year he is wondering if he can get hands enough to brand all his calves. This has been a remarkable easy winter on cattle, and the grass will be here in a few more days. Last year the sun appeared to have formed a lasting partnership with the northern icebergs and agreed to send out no more warm rays. Let us hope that our stockmen will always feel as good as they do now.—[Barber Co., Kan., Index.
articles.summary: Clipped stock news: English cattle-import protests, Kansas cattle disease, Oregon horse disease, and a cheerful Barber County cattleman.
Filler anecdote about a Leominster farmer curing a balky horse by leaving it alone (not transcribed).

articles.headline: DICKINSON NOTES.
articles.text:
DICKINSON, April 9, 1884.

The presence of Messrs. Bramble & Keyes on Monday gave our townspeople renewed interest in the proposed freight route, and we expect to see before long a few, at least, of the thousand teams that are said to be at work on the line.

Private teams have been loaded out for the Hills right along and more freight on the way.

Large quantities of nursery goods in the shape of orchard and garden fruit trees from New York and Illinois nurseries are lying in the freight house.

It is said that steps will be taken during the week looking toward the erection of a capacious warehouse at this point to accommodate the Black Hills freight.

Dickinson is growing. Several men have come here during the week past who expect to remain. One of them has bought a lot and a bill of lumber, and will put up his house himself immediately. Another gentleman, Dr. Pelton, of Frederick City, Md., looking up land and investments in his own interest and eastern parties, has written for them to come on. The doctor is a practical man and proposes to employ steam to break the Dakota sod, also to grind feed, bale hay and in various other ways make the invisible giant useful. He expects to use a convertible traction engine instead of the cable system in use elsewhere.

We observed the polite reference to our former notes in The Dickinson Press of the 5th inst. In the spasm of courtesy that agitated the worthy editor, he entirely forgot to say that our note was untrue. We fail to see the motive that actuated him, but probably he thinks he knows the side upon which his bread is buttered, and since The Press has appropriated the issue, we will say to him that it knows the truth of the note criticised. The example of misrepresentation selected for our text is only one of many such which will some day rise in condemnation of their author. Of course, if the authors alone were the ones who would suffer, no one would care to stay the coming retribution, but they are not; this whole country and the people who are misled are the ones to suffer. Intelligent selfishness alone ought to instruct thinking men better. The very lax ideas of business morality indicated by such methods must be corrected, otherwise they will correct themselves in a fashion not altogether to the fancy of such business men. And when a so-called newspaper prostitutes its pages to support and intrench what it knows to be false, it simply shows the depth to which the disease of commercial immorality has burrowed.

ANTHROPOS.
articles.summary: Dickinson correspondent 'Anthropos' on the freight route, Black Hills freight, new settlers and a quarrel with The Dickinson Press.

articles.text: Mr. Boice, of the well-known firm of Berry, Boice & Co., says that although many weak pilgrims were brought into this country late last fall, the total loss of cattle for the Bad Lands will fall considerably under three per cent.

articles.text: Mr. G. Grisy, of Grisy and Wibaux, is enthusiastic over this as a cattle country. He has only been here a year but his herd is in splendid condition and his loss will fall under one per cent. We doubt if a better showing can be found anywhere.
articles.summary: Grisy of Grisy and Wibaux reports loss under one per cent.

articles.text: Jos. Doulische, who was considered almost well from the injuries he received from the caving in of a foundation, died last Thursday. His death was entirely unexpected and was a great blow to the family. He was buried Saturday afternoon on the coal mine butte.
articles.summary: Jos. Doulische died of injuries from a foundation cave-in and was buried on the coal mine butte.

articles.text: Gregor Lang had a valuable horse stolen from the Cantonment last Saturday night, but it was tracked and recovered thirty-five miles up the river, the first of the week. We profess to be a law-abiding citizen but we wish to state here and now that the most effectual way of ridding the country of horse thieves is to hang them when caught, to the nearest tree. We have been remarkably [free?] from such depredators and harsh measures will insure immunity for the future.
articles.summary: Gregor Lang's horse stolen and recovered; Packard urges hanging horse thieves.

articles.text: Two hundred and sixty head of yearlings and two-year-olds, belonging to W. N. Thompson & Co., came in yesterday morning. They were under the charge of Wm. Dantz and Lloyd Roberts, who brought them through from Minnesota. They were in prime condition, although they had a long run from Jamestown. Yesterday afternoon they were started toward the home ranch. Messrs. Dantz and Roberts will return soon to Minnesota after another bunch. Meantime, the former will go into the upper country after horses.
articles.summary: 260 head of W. N. Thompson & Co. cattle arrived from Minnesota.

articles.text: Another good citizen will soon be lost and gained, Mandan being the loser and Medora the gainer. Mr. Book came last Friday and was satisfied far beyond his expectations. The supposition was that good brick clay was here in abundance, but we confess that we were surprised to find the value of our buttes. Clay for making the best red and cream-colored brick in the world is here in the greatest abundance. Mr. Book says that he can compete [in every?] way with St. Louis and Milwaukee brick, pressed or moulded. Besides these kinds of clay, Mr. Book discovered the best quality of fire clay. This will be extremely valuable, as it is and has always been costly. Beyond this, too, was the discovery of cement and a vein of pottery clay that surpasses anything found anywhere. At last the Bad Lands are coming to the front as being something besides the best cattle country in the United States, and Mr. Book proposes to help develop them to their utmost. He is now in Mandan getting his outfit ready and will soon be here and at work. His first contract is for 500,000 brick for the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co., but others will soon keep him busy. In the fall he will start an extensive pottery works, thus furnishing employment to many men the year round. Mr. Book is thoroughly in earnest in this matter and is sure of great success.
articles.summary: Brick maker Mr. Book to move from Mandan to Medora; first contract 500,000 brick for the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.

articles.text: A large cinnamon bear, weight about 1,200 pounds, was killed lately near J. A. Beaumont's sheep ranch. "Scotty" has promised us the claws and if they don't materialize pretty soon, we intend starting after them.
articles.summary: Large cinnamon bear killed near J. A. Beaumont's sheep ranch.

articles.text: With ten changes of horses, it took the last mail on the Pierre line nearly seven days to get into the Hills. Messrs. Jones, Louthan, Jorgan and Deffebach came through in three days and a half with no change of horses. Our route is dry and dusty. The Pierre route is a perfect quagmire of gumbo.
articles.summary: Pierre mail line took seven days to the Hills; the Medora route party took three and a half.

articles.text: Of all the dismal failures we ever saw, the bear and boar fight last Saturday was the worst. The two bears and boar being put into a cattle car, the only sign of hostility between them was a sigh of satisfaction on the part of the boar as he nestled down in the soft fur of one of the bears, who had previously curled up into one of the corners and gone to sleep.
articles.summary: Bear and boar fight in a cattle car a dismal failure.

articles.text: Dr. Louthan added materially to the value of our Bad Lands museum by presenting us with some fine specimens of petrified eels and the petrified coccyx of a human being, probably an Indian woman. He also gave us a specimen of coal from a mine on our freight route which is pure anthracite of a quality very nearly, if not quite, equal to Pennsylvania coal.
articles.summary: Dr. Louthan gave fossils and coal specimens to the Bad Lands museum.

articles.text: The western line of Dakota, running due south forms the eastern Wyoming line. Medora and Deadwood are both almost exactly fifteen miles from this line. Medora, therefore, is almost if not directly on a line drawn directly north from Deadwood. Except for about four miles in the Bad Lands and another short turn near Spearfish, our route goes almost as straight as the flight of a bullet. Accurate judges estimate the distance at one hundred and seventy-two miles.
articles.summary: Medora is almost due north of Deadwood; route estimated at 172 miles.

articles.text: Let every Republican heed the call published elseywhere and attend the convention to be held day after to-morrow in Medora, at the Hotel de Mores, at 2 P. M. For many reasons a full attendance is necessary, to express the will of the majority of the Republican voters, to elect a good delegate to Huron and a good county central committee, to have every voter's political status decided, to form a union so that concerted action can be taken and to consider many other items of interest that will turn up.
articles.summary: Packard urges Republicans to attend Saturday's convention at the Hotel de Mores.

articles.text: The most complete success in the amusement way we have ever had was the stockmen's ball last Saturday evening, given by Messrs. Keeler and Goodall. The music was furnished by Messrs. R. A. Dickinson and R. D. Owen, of Glendive, on violins, and T. J. Kerr on the piano. No one could possibly pick a flaw in the music and all three of the gentlemen showed that they were finished musicians. They can consider themselves engaged for future events of the kind. The ladies turned out in full force and joined in the good time as heartily as the gentlemen. The climax was reached, however, when the company seated themselves to as fine a supper as could be gotten up in the west. Everything that heart could wish was provided in abundance and keen appetites soon made large inroads on the choice viands. No expense was spared to make the ball a success, which it was in every sense of the word.
articles.summary: Stockmen's ball given by Keeler and Goodall was a great success.

articles.text: A Connecticut emigrant standing on the platform of a train yesterday began to remark that "This seems to be a pooty slim kentry," when seeing the Senate sign he started with a comrade after an invigorator. Placing ten cents on the counter, the clerical Jim remarked, "Fifteen cents more, please." The wooden nutmegger said: "What, fifteen cents for two glasses of beer?" Jim then explained that it was fifteen cents for one drink, but owing to the flush times and on account of the customer's good looks, he would break over a life-long custom make it two for a quarter, as nickels did not pass here. And then the emigrant wrapped his arms around his stomach and is probably hugging it yet to get his money's worth out of that beer. We wonder what he will say when he bumps up against "a quarter a smile" in Montana.
articles.summary: Anecdote of a Connecticut emigrant and beer prices at the Senate.

articles.headline: BELFIELD GOSSIP.
articles.text:
BELFIELD, Dak., April 9, 1884.

EDITOR COW BOY:

May!

May she never!

May she never return!

Breaking, seeding and backsetting are now in full blast, and it now looks as if mother earth would be afforded every opportunity to distinguish herself this season.

Wm. LeMoyne returned east Sunday morning in company of a Mr. C. Taylor, who spent several days in the village.

Postmaster Harbison left for his former home in New York a few days ago. He intends to go into a limited partnership (for life) bringing with him Mrs. J. W. Harbison upon his return. All the available tin cans, pans and such will be brought into requisition to properly serenade the happy couple upon their arrival at Belfield!

The "cause celebre" of the stolen pony was settled by the Townsite Company paying costs and furnishing a good substitute for the replevined animal.

Several couples prepared to attend the ball at Little Missouri Saturday, but the long delay of a freight train finally kept many at home who now deeply regret their change of base. Those who were fortunate enough to attend pronounce the affair the most enjoyable ever held west of the Missouri and sincerely hope for a repetition of the good time.

Bob Montgomery has just finished his spring cleaning and those who knew his place before will have visions of Arabian nights when they enter it again. A very liberal and judicious expenditure of paste, brush and paper coupled with Mr. Day's artistic skill have transformed his neat resort into one of the cosiest places on the line, and the vicious buffalo who holds the fort, more loudly than words proclaims "Get there, Eli."

Bob Tuttle has had word sent him from the Indian agency that he can have his stolen horses returned to him by calling for them at the agency. Bob will go, and if he meets the fellows who took accidentally, there will be some more good Indians added to the list.

Quite a heavy delegation of Belfielders will likely attend Saturday's first convention of Billings county.

Ed. Gallien proved up on his valuable homestead a few days ago, making the third homestead proved up on at Belfield within four months.

United States Government Surveyor Austin visited the town on Saturday and the result will be that three new townships will be surveyed in a few weeks. This land comprises some of the very finest in the county and will not go begging a minute.

SADIE.
articles.summary: Belfield correspondent 'Sadie' on spring farming, Postmaster Harbison's wedding trip, stolen horses, homesteads and a government survey.
